paper_metadata.title: A quantum unstructured search algorithm for discrete optimisation: the use case of portfolio optimisation

summary: The paper proposes QSERA, a Grover-based quantum unstructured search method for discrete optimization, and demonstrates it on a 4-asset portfolio problem with 4 data qubits plus 3 ancillas (7 qubits total). The example uses a zero-noise Qiskit simulator, 2 Grover iterations for the 16-state search space, and a classically constructed oracle with assumed fmin = 0 and fmax = 0.15; no practical quantum advantage is demonstrated.

experiments.description: QSERA gate-based Grover search applied to a 4-asset portfolio optimization instance, using an oracle built from the objective function and Grover amplitude amplification to identify the minimum.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Search for Extrema and Roots Algorithm (QSERA) using Grover's algorithm
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Use mopt ≃ (π√N − 2)/4 Grover iterations; for the 4-asset example N=16 so mopt=2
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Oracle parameters derived classically from the objective function coefficients; Grover register initialized in uniform superposition

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 4 binary variables xa, xb, xc, xd encode whether each of the 4 assets is selected; portfolios are represented as 4-bit strings bdbcbbba / |bdbcbbba⟩
problem_formulation.objective_function: f(xa, xb, xc, xd) = λµ (Npµp − Npµb)^2 + λσ2 (N_p^2σ_p^2 − N_p^2σ_b^2)^2 + (1 − λµ − λσ2)(Np − Nb)^2, with Np = xa+xb+xc+xd, µp and σp defined from asset returns/volatilities/correlations
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Soft penalty term (1 − λµ − λσ2)(Np − Nb)^2 enforces target number of assets Nb=2

problem_instance.description: Toy portfolio optimization benchmark with 4 assets (a,b,c,d) and target benchmark return/volatility

dataset_specification.benchmark_name: benchmark portfolio with µb=0.043 and σb=0.195

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Exhaustive evaluation over all 2^4 = 16 portfolios; probability distribution of measured states after Grover iterations; single-shot and repeated-shot discussion

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classically compute objective-function coefficients, rescale f(x) to g(x), then recursively compute coefficients of g(x)^n for oracle construction
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measure bitstrings and identify the most probable portfolio; multiple shots suggested when fmin/fmax are approximated

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: Grover amplitude amplification increases target-state probability up to mopt, then becomes periodic

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical brute-force search over an unordered list
speedup_claims.conditions: when fmin and fmax are known a priori and the oracle is exact; Grover iterations scale as O(sqrt(N))
speedup_claims.caveats: For approximate fmin/fmax, the target-state probability can be less than 1; multiple shots may be needed. The paper also notes that if n is too large and fmin/fmax are misestimated, un(z) can go to 0 for all z.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; only a 4-asset / 16-state toy instance is shown.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require a much larger problem instance, exact oracle construction, and fault-tolerant Grover iterations; the paper does not provide a practical resource estimate.
limiting_factors: Only a zero-noise simulator is used
Oracle construction requires prior knowledge of fmin and fmax
Oracle coefficients for g(x)^n are computed classically
No runtime or wall-clock comparison against classical methods

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states the quantum computations were performed on a classical computer using a zero-noise simulator from Qiskit.
num_qubits inferred from 4 data qubits for the 4 assets plus 3 ancilla qubits (two ancilla for AND operators and one phase ancilla) described in the circuit section.
circuit_depth not explicitly reported; only the Grover iteration count mopt=2 and circuit decomposition are given.
The paper presents QSERA as a theoretical algorithm and a simulator-based demonstration, not as an empirical quantum advantage result.
Classical exhaustive search is used only as a conceptual baseline; no measured performance comparison is reported.
